title: Without Entropy, There Would Be No Life
subtitle: Evolution depends on entropy
author: Avshalom Elitzur
introduction: Order and chaos are concepts used in everything from theoretical physics to psychology. But are order and disorder built into the fabric of reality itself, or are they just concepts that humans use to make sense of the world? In this interview with physicist Avshalom Elitzur, he argues the physics behind the 2nd law of thermodynamics is indisputable, and explores the implications this has for the future, and possible end, of humanity.
body:
This article is presented in association with Closer To Truth, a partner for HowTheLightGetsIn Festival 2024.

What is entropy and why is it essential to our understanding of the universe?

Entropy is something very peculiar. Let's remember that all physical quantities are conserved: In any closed system, energy is conserved, matter is conserved, momentum is conserved. That means that these values do not vanish and are not created anew.

There is, however, one value which is not conserved, and this is entropy.

Now the question is, what is entropy? There are several definitions or measures.

  1. The simplest, and most intuitive, is disorder. Some scientists do not like this definition because they say it's subjective. Other scientists propose some other definitions. I think that disorder is a fairly good definition. But to be more precise, let us give two more definitions:

  2. Entropy goes up every time that something irreversible happens. A hot cup of coffee disperses heat into the room's air. You will never see a cup of coffee sucking heat from its surroundings. Or you spill milk, and you know that you will never see this milk going back into your bottle. Similarly for a candle being burnt: you will never see all the particles of smoke coming back into the flame and giving you the white wax again. This is also very intuitive and nice.

  3. An akin definition of entropy is equilibrium. Think of a teenager's closet. Make it highly ordered. You have all the shirts on one place, on the trousers on another place, underwear on another shelf. "Ordered" then means "far from equilibrium." Now take again the above hot coffee. You begin with all heat concentrated in the coffee and end up with the heat evenly spread all over. Similarly for the milk, candle etc.

  4. Entropy has the highest probability. First let me stress that if any of the above unlikely events (disordered closet becoming ordered by the teenager's unintended use; milk unsplit; candle unburned; etc.) happens, there will be no violation of conservation laws! Energy will be conserved, matter will be conserved, etc. Why, then, do they not occur? Because they are extremely unlikely! Very rarely you will see small reversals of entropy, but only at the microscopic level, i.e. a few molecules. The more molecules involved in the process, the greater the unlikelihood of its reversal. You have to wait billions of billions of years to see such a rare event.

See how all these measures converge? There are a few more. All are different facets of the same thing.

You mention several different definitions of entropy. Is there an objective one?

They are all objective! And moreover complement one another. It depends whether you are a physicist, a mathematician, an engineer, or a chemist. So when I teach thermodynamics, rather than going into the tiring debates which is the best definition, I just teach them all, and then I show that they give you a beautiful, intuitive picture which is very profound.

Switching gears to the Second Law of Thermodynamics: How does entropy relate to the second law?

Simple: It is the Second Law of Thermodynamics that dictates that in every closed system, entropy can go only up, or – if it's maximal – remain the same.

What is the evidence that we have for the Second Law?

Everywhere! From the moment we began this conversation entropy has increased everywhere within us and in all our surroundings. Your body has dispersed heat. Similarly for the Sun, dispersing heat to Earth which dispersed heat back to empty space, and all the processes fueled by this heat dispersal obey the Second Law.

SUGGESTED READING Time is the increase of order, not disorder By Julian Barbour

So that's the empirical evidence, which you'll see in physics, cosmology, biology, chemistry and everywhere. Mathematically, you can make calculations. You count the number of ingredients of a system, then you count the number of possible arrangements of these ingredients. And then mathematics shows you that entropy increase is the most likely outcome.

We know that random mutations in DNA add up to create very ordered structures, like the eyeball, wings, and the human brain. Might life on Earth, specifically the fact that life evolves to be more ordered over time rather than more disordered, a counter example to the Second Law?

Absolutely not! If the Second Law were not valid, there would be no life. We depend on entropy. Remember that the Second Law says that in every closed system, entropy goes up. We are by no means closed systems: We breathe, eat, go to the bathroom, etc., so matter and energy come in and out. It is therefore only locally that entropy is decreasing in our bodies. We increase order in our body, and we increase complexity, which is somewhat akin to order, but we pay for it. And the price is that entropy in our surroundings goes up.

Evolution depends on entropy in two ways. One, you need mutations in the DNA. DNA is replicated from one generation to the other, but there are always mutations. Mutations are noise, which is just another word for entropy. Here, in fact, is another definition of entropy in terms of information theory. Noise is then a manifestation of entropy. Had there been no mutations, there would be no evolution and no life. And entropy helps you also in the other way: Most of these mutations perish. They therefore succumb to the Second Law. So again, you have entropy increase. Think about all the dinosaurs which perished, they increased entropy on Earth. A much-much larger number of organisms and species perished from the beginning of life on Earth, in comparison to the tiny fraction of those who survive and multiply. So entropy shapes life on both sides, from the very beginning by mutations and at the end by natural selection.

There is a beautiful verse in Faust by Goethe. Faust asks the devil who he is, and the devil tells him: "I am part of nature that always wills to produce evil but brings the good.”

People may not like what I say. We are in a time in which humanity is in huge danger.

We are running a debate this year that's entitled The World of Order and Chaos at the HowTheLightGetsIn festival, which is about whether order and disorder are embedded into the fabric of reality, or whether these are just concepts that we use to make sense of the world, but that don't really exist.

They are objective! Just as energy and mass are objective. You can measure them, and you can measure entropy mathematically. By dividing temperature with heat. And it is so precise that two different scientists, even from different disciplines, if you show them a certain process or a certain calculation, they will agree how much entropy has increased. Entropy as a measure, just like length and weight. Here is an example: You introduce some heat to a system. You measure the heat, and then you measure the system's temperature after a while. If it's a big system, then the increase in temperature will be small, right? And that means that entropy has increased a lot. You had all the heat being concentrated when you entered it to the system, and then it got dispersed. It's mathematics.

namely, divide the energy inserted to the system by its temperature. The mathematics is not really hard, and makes much sense.

How do we know that we're getting something that's really built into the fabric of reality, that's built into the nature of existence itself? How do we know that we're not actually just dealing with a concept that humans impose?

But you could ask the same question for the conservation of energy!

That’s right. I'm asking about any physical quantity.

So that's a different issue. You may ask me, how do you define mass? And I can tell you, this is some convention we have. You must begin with some convention, whether you want to define mass by kilograms, by libras, or by something else. Different civilizations, different cultures, will have different units, but that's irrelevant. The moment you agree on some units, this is where science and physics begin to advance. Your questions are not about entropy. They are just about physics. In physics, once we agree on a convention, we get a very solid and rigourous science.

It is the first time in the history of this globe, in 4 billion years, that entropy is remaining with us.

Should we consider abandoning this framework of order and chaos and order and disorder?

No, you're abandoning science if you do that! Let me tell you where entropy becomes extremely crucial for our very future. People may not like what I say. We are in a time in which humanity is in huge danger. Ecology tells us that we are almost doomed. Look what happens at the time that we are talking. For the first time in history, there is a huge fire in the Amazon, which is the very lungs of Earth! This has been the hottest summer ever. There are some idiots – please make sure to quote me correctly – some morons that claim that the global warming is just a hoax and that it's not real science and so on. This is the dumbest thing that you can think of! There is a consensus all over by all universities, all scientists, that something very bad is happening to the biosphere and that this is our doing! We have to take care of it. This is directly relevant to our discussion of entropy increasing.

SUGGESTED READING Lee Smolin: the laws of the universe are changing By Lee Smolin

So let me give you an example, and this is something which Penrose has made a very beautiful analysis of: For 4 billion years, we had energy coming from the Sun to Earth, and then energy leaving Earth back to space. Here is the important thing. We get energy coming from the Sun closer to the blue light range. These are fewer photons with shorter wavelengths. They come, we absorb them when we eat food. And then we radiate electromagnetic radiation back to outer space, but this radiation is more red: More photons with a longer wavelength. Entropy is increasing, but in an interesting way, such that most of the entropy goes to the outer space. It is the first time in the history of this globe, in 4 billion years, that entropy is remaining with us. Think about the plastic and the CO2. These are things that don't leave us, and the heat is not leaving us. Thermodynamics is extremely important for the nature of humanity because it bears directly to ecology and environmental science.

Thank you very much, Avshalom.

With pleasure.
